paragraphs: The sky above your home belongs to a much larger story. What can a careful observer discover in it?

Yangdol and her twin brother Dorjay live in Nubra, Ladakh. On a clear evening, they sit outside with an adult and watch stars appear. Mountains frame their view. On other nights, clouds, moonlight or nearby lamps make some stars harder to see.

Their elders tell stories about patterns in the stars and travellers who used the sky to find directions. The twins begin asking their own questions. Are the bright points all stars? Why do some patterns seem to move? What lies beyond the objects they can see?

Begin with observations from Earth, then travel in thought through our Solar System and into the Milky Way. Use patterns as guides, distinguish a model from the real sky, and keep track of what evidence can tell us.

lesson.text: 12.1 Stars and Their Patterns

At night, some points of light look bright and others faint. **Stars** produce their own light. A star’s apparent brightness depends on its light output and its distance from us, as well as conditions along the way. A brighter-looking star is not necessarily nearer or larger than every faint one.

paragraphs: 1. Look at the unconnected points below. Copy their arrangement into your notebook. This is a drawing exercise, not a map for finding a real constellation.
2. Imagine an object or animal suggested by some points. Join your chosen points with lines and name your pattern. Try a second pattern using the same points.
3. Compare with a partner. Which points did you choose? Tell a short story about your pattern, and distinguish the invented story from the dots you both observed.
lesson.diagramCaption: Fig. 12.1 · One arrangement can suggest different pictures.

lesson.text: People in many cultures imagined shapes among the stars and used them to remember parts of the sky. The joining lines are not objects in space. Stars that look close together in a pattern may actually be at very different distances from Earth. A pattern is a view from here, not a group tied together by lines.

Astronomers now divide the whole sky into 88 defined regions called **constellations**. Familiar patterns often lie within these regions. A well-known pattern that is not itself an entire constellation is called an **asterism**. The Big Dipper, for example, is part of the constellation Ursa Major.

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.2 · Selected stars near Orion and Taurus. Lines are guides; orientations change as the sky turns.

lesson.text: Orion’s three belt stars form a short, nearly straight row. Betelgeuse lies towards one shoulder; Rigel marks one foot in the traditional figure. Nearby in the sky, Sirius belongs to Canis Major. Sirius is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky, although the Sun appears much brighter by day.

Different traditions give these objects different names. Betelgeuse is associated with Ardra, Aldebaran with Rohini, and the Pleiades star cluster with Krittika in Indian astronomical traditions. These examples do not make every traditional sky division identical to a modern constellation. Ask which actual star, group or sky region a name refers to.

The Big Dipper’s seven main stars make a bowl and handle. It is also known as Saptarishi. The Little Dipper is part of Ursa Minor; Polaris, the **Pole Star**, is at the end of its handle. Polaris is also called Dhruva tara. Stories may help us remember the shapes, while measurements help us locate the stars.
12.2 Preparing to Watch the Sky

What you can see depends on your location, date, time, weather and view of the horizon. Buildings or trees may hide a target. Scattered light from lamps can wash out faint stars; bright moonlight can do so too. Not seeing a star on one night is not evidence that it has stopped shining.

Unwanted or excessive artificial light at night contributes to **light pollution**. Shielding lights downwards, choosing suitable brightness and using them only when needed can reduce it. Keep lighting required for safety. A dark-sky site protects useful darkness; it is not necessarily free of clouds or air pollution.

paragraphs: Plan a safe observation with an adult, using a current sky map for your place and time. A printed chart or a tool such as Stellarium can help. Check directions and the horizon before looking for a target.
Allow your eyes time to adjust to darkness and keep screens dim. Begin with unaided eyes. A telescope gathers light and can reveal detail, but it needs careful aiming and adult guidance.
lesson.caption: Fig. 12.3 · A small refracting telescope. An instrument does not replace careful identification.

lesson.text: Never look directly at the Sun, or point binoculars or a telescope at it. Ordinary sunglasses do not make this safe. All observing activities here are for the night sky, with an adult present, from safe ground away from roads, roofs and steep edges.
Finding the Pole Star

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.4 · Follow the bowl’s two pointer stars towards Polaris. Pattern orientation varies; lines are imaginary.

paragraphs: 1. With an adult, use a sky map to choose a date and evening time when the Big Dipper is above your northern horizon. In much of India, suitable spring or summer evenings can be useful; verify your location.
2. Find the bowl and handle. Identify Merak and Dubhe, the two stars at the outer end of the bowl. Compare the pattern with Fig. 12.4 rather than choosing any bright pair.
3. Continue the direction from Merak through Dubhe for about five times their separation beyond Dubhe. Look for Polaris near that line and confirm it with the chart.
4. Sketch what you could identify, recording time, direction and conditions. If the target is hidden or too faint, record that; do not claim a successful identification without evidence.

lesson.text: Polaris lies close to the direction of Earth’s north rotation axis, so it appears nearly stationary while other stars seem to circle that direction. It indicates approximately north from places in the Northern Hemisphere. It is not the brightest star, and it is normally below the horizon in the Southern Hemisphere.
Following Orion’s Belt

paragraphs: 1. Ask an adult to check when Orion is visible after sunset at your location. Winter and early-spring evenings are often suitable in India; use the actual date and time, not a fixed promise.
2. Find the three belt stars and compare the surrounding bright stars with Fig. 12.2. Match the whole pattern before naming it.
3. Extend the belt line in the direction shown towards Sirius, away from the Taurus side. Rotate the chart to match your view; “left” or “right” on the page is not a fixed direction in the sky.
4. Record the date, time and what you identified. Compare with the chart and explain any uncertainty, cloud cover or obstruction.

lesson.text: A sky chart predicts where an object should appear for stated conditions. Your notes record what you actually saw. If the two differ, check time, location, viewing direction and obstacles before deciding the chart is wrong. A missing observation can be informative when its limits are recorded.
12.3 Our Solar System

paragraphs: The **Sun** is our nearest star. It is an enormous, very hot sphere, mostly hydrogen and helium. Nuclear fusion in its interior releases energy that eventually leaves as light and other radiation. It is not an ordinary fire burning in air.

Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun on average. This distance is approximately one astronomical unit, or au. The Sun’s diameter is about 109 times Earth’s, yet it looks small because it is far away.
lesson.caption: Fig. 12.5 · An illustrated Sun. Never observe it directly with your eyes or ordinary optical equipment.

lesson.text: Other stars are so much farther away that they appear as points. During the day, sunlight scattered by Earth’s atmosphere makes the sky bright and overwhelms their faint light. The stars have not switched off. After the Sun, the nearest star to us is Proxima Centauri, more than four light-years away.

Sunlight powers photosynthesis and helps drive weather and the water cycle. Earth’s rotation gives us the daily pattern of daylight and darkness. Seasons depend on Earth’s tilted axis as it travels around the Sun, not simply on being nearer to the Sun. These changes will be explored more fully in Class 7.

Our **Solar System** contains the Sun and the objects bound to it by gravity, including eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets. In this system, a planet orbits the Sun, is nearly round under its own gravity and has cleared its orbital neighbourhood. “Cleared” means it is gravitationally dominant there, not that its path is perfectly empty.

lesson.caption: Table 12.1 · Turning and travelling
rows: A solar day is about 24 hours
Travelling around another body in an orbit
One orbit around the Sun takes about a year
lesson.note: Earth turns while it revolves. These are different motions happening together.

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.6 · Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, in order from the Sun. Displayed sizes and spacing are not to scale.

lesson.text: The four inner planets—**Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars**—have rocky surfaces. Mercury is nearest the Sun. Venus is covered by thick clouds. Earth has extensive surface oceans. Rust-coloured materials on Mars help give it the name Red Planet. Similar membership in a group does not mean identical conditions.

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.7 · Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune follow the inner four. Displayed sizes and spacing are not to scale.
Table 12.2 · Comparing groups of planets
rows: Relatively small, with solid rocky surfaces
Very large; mainly hydrogen and helium
Rich in materials such as water, ammonia and methane beneath their atmospheres
lesson.note: “Ice giant” describes composition; it does not mean a solid frozen surface you could stand on.

lesson.text: All four giant planets have rings, though Saturn’s are easiest to recognise. Rings contain many separate particles; they are not solid hoops. Saturn’s bright rings are mainly water ice, with some rocky material and dust. The giant planets also have many natural satellites.

Distance affects the sunlight a planet receives, but atmosphere matters too. Venus’s thick atmosphere traps heat, making its surface hotter than Mercury’s even though Venus is farther from the Sun. One factor alone is not enough to explain every planet’s temperature.

Pluto is a **dwarf planet**, not one of the eight planets. It orbits the Sun and is nearly round, but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood. Dwarf planets remain members of the Solar System. Being small by itself is not the whole definition; Ceres in the asteroid belt is another dwarf planet.
Identifying a Planet in the Sky

Planets seen with unaided eyes usually appear as points reflecting sunlight. Venus is often very bright and is sometimes called the Morning Star or Evening Star, although it is a planet. It is not visible at both times on every date. Mercury, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can also be visible without a telescope when conditions are suitable.

paragraphs: 1. Ask an adult to use a current sky map to select a date when Venus is well placed after sunset or before sunrise. Do not search while the Sun is above the horizon.
2. For an evening appearance, check the western sky after sunset. For a morning appearance, check the eastern sky before sunrise and stop before the Sun rises. Use unaided eyes only.
3. Record direction, time and the bright point’s position relative to a fixed landmark. Confirm the identification using the chart. Do not infer that every bright point near the horizon is Venus.
4. Repeat on another suitable date if possible. Note conditions and whether the predicted object was visible. Stay with your accompanying adult throughout.

lesson.text: Stars often twinkle more than planets because turbulent air changes how their tiny points of light reach us. Planets have a small apparent disc, so these changes tend to average out. This is a clue, not a certain test: planets can twinkle, especially near the horizon. Use position and a sky map as further evidence.
The Moon and Other Satellites

paragraphs: A **natural satellite**, or moon, orbits a larger body. Earth has one natural Moon; Mars has two. Mercury and Venus have none. Some moons are larger than Mercury, so it is wrong to say every moon is smaller than every planet.

Our Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from Earth on average, with a diameter about one-quarter of Earth’s. It shines mainly by reflecting sunlight. Its orbit around Earth takes about 27.3 days relative to the distant stars.
lesson.caption: Fig. 12.8 · Dark plains and impact craters mark the Moon’s surface.

lesson.text: The Moon’s sunlit half is viewed from changing angles as it orbits Earth, giving us its phases. The familiar new-Moon-to-new-Moon cycle takes about 29.5 days because Earth is moving around the Sun too. The phase cycle and the orbital period are related but are not the same interval. Phases are not ordinarily caused by Earth’s shadow.

Many bowl-shaped lunar craters were made by impacts from space rocks. The Moon has a very thin exosphere rather than Earth’s substantial atmosphere, and lacks Earth-like rain and flowing surface water to wear features away quickly. Water ice occurs in some permanently shadowed polar places; “no water anywhere on the Moon” would be incorrect.

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.9 · Artist’s impression of a lunar lander and rover, not a construction diagram.

lesson.text: India launched Chandrayaan-1 in 2008 and Chandrayaan-2 in 2019. Chandrayaan-3’s Vikram lander, carrying the Pragyan rover, made a successful soft landing in the Moon’s southern high-latitude region on 23 August 2023. The date is observed as National Space Day. A landing in that region is not a landing at the exact south pole.

Space missions answer questions using instruments, measurements and carefully interpreted images. A photograph alone cannot show everything about a world. To learn about a later mission or a proposed sample-return mission, check ISRO’s current information and distinguish an announced plan from a completed result.
Asteroids and Comets

lesson.caption: Table 12.3 · Two kinds of small Solar System bodies
rows: Where or how it is seen
Mainly rock and/or metal; many are irregular
Many orbit in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter
Ices, dust and rocky material; can develop a coma and tails
Some become active when they approach the Sun
lesson.note: There are exceptions and transitional objects; neither group is identified by shape alone.

lesson.text: The main asteroid belt contains many separated objects, not a tightly packed wall of rocks. Some asteroids orbit elsewhere, including near Earth’s orbit. They cover a wide range of sizes; the larger ones can be nearly round. A drawing of the belt usually exaggerates both asteroid size and crowding so that the objects can be seen.

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.10 · Artist’s impression of an active comet. Its nucleus is much smaller than the surrounding coma and tails.

lesson.text: When a comet is warmed by the Sun, some ice changes directly into gas, releasing dust. This forms a surrounding **coma**. Sunlight and the solar wind push material generally away from the Sun, forming tails. A tail is not a trail of fire, and it does not simply point backwards along the comet’s path.

Some comets return periodically; others may escape, break apart or collide with another body. Halley’s comet takes roughly 76 years per orbit and last passed through the inner Solar System in 1986. A comet’s appearance is a natural event, not evidence that it causes good or bad luck.
12.4 Our Home Galaxy

From a sufficiently dark location, part of the Milky Way can appear as a faint band across the sky. Its position and visibility depend on season, time and location; it is not always a fixed north-to-south stripe. We see this band because we look through many stars and clouds within our galaxy’s disc.

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.11 · Artist’s external view of a spiral galaxy. We cannot take this outside view of our own galaxy from Earth.

lesson.text: A **galaxy** is an enormous system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity. The **Milky Way Galaxy**, also called Akasha Ganga, is our home galaxy. Our Solar System is one small part of it, away from its centre. The bright sky band and the entire galaxy are related, but are not identical views.
12.5 A Universe to Investigate

Many galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way. The **Universe** includes space, time and all the matter and energy within it. Telescopes and other instruments gather evidence from far beyond what unaided eyes can see. Diagrams that place Earth, the Solar System and the Milky Way inside larger groups show membership, not physical walls.

lesson.caption: Fig. 12.12 · Follow the membership chain. These are not relative sizes or distances.

lesson.text: Scientists investigate whether life exists beyond Earth, including on worlds in our Solar System and on **exoplanets**, planets orbiting other stars. No life beyond Earth has yet been confirmed. Finding water or a possible chemical clue is not the same as confirming life; several explanations must be tested.

paragraphs: A headline says, “Water detected on a distant world: life discovered!” Which part could be an observation, and which is an unsupported conclusion? Suggest one further question scientists would need to investigate.

lesson.text: Yangdol and Dorjay cannot visit every world they have read about. They can still ask useful questions, compare predictions with observations, and change an explanation when evidence demands it. Their next clear evening begins with a small task: choose one object, check when it is visible, and make a careful record.

glossary.purpose: Reference definitions for terms taught in the chapter
entries: An object that produces its own light through processes within it.
One of the 88 defined regions of the sky.
A recognisable star pattern, such as the Big Dipper.
Polaris, near the direction of Earth’s north rotation axis.
Unwanted or excessive artificial light at night.
About 150 million km, roughly the mean Earth–Sun distance.
Motion around another body along an orbit.
In our system, a nearly round Sun-orbiting body dominant in its orbital neighbourhood.
A naturally occurring body orbiting a larger body.
The Sun and objects gravitationally bound to it.
A small body, mainly rock or metal, orbiting the Sun.
An icy body that can develop a coma and tails near the Sun.
A vast system of stars and other matter bound by gravity.
A planet orbiting a star other than the Sun.
All space, time, matter and energy.

summary: Stars produce their own light. Apparent patterns do not mean their stars are close together in space.
The sky has 88 constellation regions. The Big Dipper is an asterism within Ursa Major.
Polaris appears nearly stationary near the north celestial pole. A current chart helps identify it from the Northern Hemisphere.
Sky visibility depends on place, date, time and conditions. Observe with an adult and never look directly at the Sun.
The Sun is our nearest star. Scattered sunlight makes other stars difficult to see in the daytime sky.
The planets in order are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto is a dwarf planet.
Earth rotates while revolving around the Sun. A day and a year describe different motions.
The Moon reflects sunlight. Its orbit takes about 27.3 days; its phase cycle takes about 29.5 days.
Asteroids and comets are Solar System members. Comet tails form when sunlight and solar wind act on released material.
Our Solar System belongs to the Milky Way. Other galaxies and exoplanets exist; life beyond Earth is not yet confirmed.

assessment.purpose: All eleven source questions retained with safety and evidence qualifications

questions.text: Match each description with one item in the second column. Then explain why the name “Evening Star” can be misleading.

table.caption: Descriptions and possible matches
rows: A planet called the Evening Star
table.note: The entries across a row are not necessarily a correct pair.

questions.text: Solve this planet riddle: my first letter is in MAN but not CAN; my second is in ACE and FAN; my third is in RAT but not CAT; my fourth is in SUN but not FUN. Name the planet, then make two similar riddles about objects in space and check that each gives one clear answer.
Which is not a member of our Solar System: Sirius, comets, asteroids or Pluto? Give a reason that distinguishes a star outside our system from bodies belonging to it.
Which is not one of the eight planets: Jupiter, Pluto, Neptune or Saturn? State its correct category without saying it is outside the Solar System.
Which appears brighter from Earth at night: Polaris or Sirius? Does greater apparent brightness alone prove that a star is closer? Explain.

A learner puts these planet-name cards in order away from the Sun: Mercury, Earth, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Uranus, Saturn, Neptune. Identify the misplaced pairs and write the complete corrected sequence. Why would equally spaced cards not make an accurate distance model?
Copy this star field into your notebook. Join the stars making the Big Dipper and Little Dipper, and mark Polaris. Use Fig. 12.4 to check, then explain which two stars you would use as pointers.
questions.caption: Fig. 12.13 · The same northern stars without guide lines or names.

questions.text: In your notebook, connect the main stars of Orion in this field and label Sirius. Use the three belt stars to guide you. Compare with Fig. 12.2; do not add a physical connection between the stars in your explanation.
questions.caption: Fig. 12.14 · Recognise a pattern among selected stars.

questions.text: Stars seem to fade at dawn and reappear after dusk. Explain what changes in the sky around us. Why is “the stars turn off during the day” not a sound explanation?

With an adult, compare three or four sky-map views of the northern sky at times two hours apart on the same simulated clear night. You may use real observations only if an adult agrees and your sleep is not disrupted. Sketch the Big Dipper and Polaris, label each time and note whether the whole pattern changes position. Explain the apparent motion.
Write a poem or short story inspired by the night sky. Afterwards, underline two statements that describe observations or established facts, and mark any invented events as imagination.

projects.title: 1. Collect names and stories
projects.text: Find local-language names for planets, stars or patterns. Ask permission before recording an elder’s story, and note who or which source supplied it. Present a drawing with the name and its scientific identification where known. Keep cultural stories distinct from evidence about how the objects work.

projects.title: 2. Visit a place that explores the sky
projects.text: With an adult, investigate a planetarium, science museum or astronomy club programme. Check current arrangements before planning a visit. Prepare three questions, distinguish a projected sky show from a real observation, and report one thing you learned. Telescope viewing depends on weather and the objects above the horizon.

projects.title: 3. Examine light near your home
projects.text: From a safe place with an adult, identify a lamp that sends light where it is not needed. Research how light at night can affect people or wildlife using a reliable source. Propose one practical change, such as shielding or a suitable timer, while retaining safety lighting. Do not alter public or household electrical fittings yourself.

projects.title: 4. Why build an observatory at Hanle?
projects.text: Use information from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics to investigate Hanle’s dry high-altitude setting and observing conditions. Explain why clear nights, darkness and atmospheric conditions matter. Find out how the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve involves local people. Record the date of your source; do not assume visitor access or event times remain unchanged.
projects.caption: Fig. 12.15 · A conceptual hilltop observatory, not a portrait of a particular building.

projects.title: 5. Make a pattern you can check
projects.text: Choose a constellation pattern you have studied. Recreate its main stars with paper dots, thread or another craft material, using a chart to check their relative positions. Label the pattern and explain that the joining lines are imaginary. If using needles or scissors, work with appropriate adult help.

closing.title: Keep Asking, Keep Checking
paragraphs: This chapter closes the book, but leaves many questions open. Choose one observation from your science notebook that surprised you. What did you first think it meant? What evidence supported or changed your explanation?

Write one question you would like to investigate next. Decide what can be observed safely, what information you need, and how you would recognise an answer that does not fit your first idea. Curiosity grows stronger when it travels with careful evidence.
